examples: You may pay in cash or by credit card.
You can join tomorrow or even next week.
Which would you prefer, in person or online?
Perhaps the cause is a configuration error.
Please submit the documents in Japanese or English.
fields.explain:
The form “N、あるいは N” is common in formal announcements and instructions.
At the beginning of a sentence, “あるいは、...” carries a polite nuance of conjecture.
In alternative questions, それとも is preferred; “Xか、あるいはYか” is emphatic/written.

- A conjunction/adverb meaning “or; or else; perhaps”.
- Formal nuance, suitable for official documents, regulations, and technical descriptions.
- With “か”: use the frame “Xか、あるいはYか” to emphasize two mutually exclusive possibilities.
fields.notes:
• When listing more than 2 items, you can say: A、B、あるいはC のいずれか.
• “あるいは” can stand mid-sentence with commas before and after to separate ideas clearly.
• In technical specifications, “または” and “もしくは/あるいは” sometimes differ in scope; follow the document's conventions. explain: A choice between two things or two sides.
A stiff way of saying　「または」 ⏐ examples: 1. ファックス、あるいはメールでお知らせください。
Please let us know by fax or email.
2. 来週の火曜日の午後はどうですか。あるいは水曜日の午前でもかまいませんが・・・。
How about next Tuesday afternoon? Or Wednesday morning would also be fine…
mistakes: Wrong particle combination: (x) A あるいは B か → (o) A か、あるいは B か.
Using あるいは in a plain question sounds stiff; それとも is preferred.
Confusing the nuance with または/もしくは: at the beginning of a sentence, あるいは can express conjecture.

rows: Formal; close to あるいは

fields.meaning: at least ～, it could be worse
fields.connection: V plain form + だけましだ / N + である / Na / Aい
examples: At least you still have a job. I got fired.
My salary was cut, but at least I didn't get fired.
My apartment is small and expensive, but at least it's convenient.
fields.explain: Expresses that although a situation is not very good, the fact that it is at that level and not worse is already quite fortunate.

fields.meaning: No sooner… than…; just when you think…, …
examples: At this time of year, just when you think it's sunny, it can suddenly start raining, so why not take an umbrella?
Dad seems busy even though it's Sunday. He came back a moment ago, and then went straight out again.
This is an event that everyone from children to the elderly can enjoy.
Everything from planning to sales is handled in-house from start to finish.
From spring all the way to winter, there is never a shortage of tourists.
We handle a wide range of goods, from daily necessities to luxury items.
We built a network reaching from urban areas all the way to remote islands.
fields.explain:
Used in written language, presentations, and descriptions of services/products/targets.
N2 is usually the extreme point or a representative example of the other end of the range.
Placed before a main clause describing an all-encompassing action: 〜に至るまで + V.
Not used for step-by-step concrete physical distance; used for a general scope.
Emphasizes comprehensiveness: goes with words like幅広く,一貫して, あらゆる.

～から～に至るまで means “from ... all the way to ...”, emphasizing a scope that stretches from the starting point to the end point, usually with a formal nuance; used in explanations, reports, and advertising.
• Creates a feeling of “covering everything”, “reaching even the extreme/periphery”.
• Often used when N2 is a surprising or distant extreme, or to emphasize comprehensiveness.
• Compared with ～から～まで: more formal, with a stronger “all the way to” nuance.
• “至る” is a verb meaning “to reach (a level/point)”, used in the linking form “に至るまで”.
fields.notes:
• Choose an N1 and N2 that are opposite or far apart for good rhythm.
• When listing more than two, use “N1からN2、N3に至るまで”.
• In marketing: “企画から運用に至るまでワンストップで提供”.
• In academic writing: “古代から近代に至るまでの変遷”.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～まで: without “に至る”, the formal/comprehensive nuance is lost.
Choosing an illogical A–B pair (not two extremes) makes the sentence lose its emphatic force.
JLPT: a trap is replacing it with ～から～にかけて; if the question wants “all the way to the extreme” → choose ～に至るまで.
Using it with verbs/modifiers: it must be N + に至るまで; V does not attach directly to に至るまで.

rows: Less formal; does not stress “all the way to”
<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもから<ruby>大人<rt>おとな</rt></ruby>まで
Stresses a vague range, not just two extremes
<ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>から<ruby>昼<rt>ひる</rt></ruby>にかけて
To lead to, to reach (a result/point)
A concluding verb, not a scope construction
<ruby>交渉<rt>こうしょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>決裂<rt>けつれつ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>至<rt>いた</rt></ruby>る
Covering everything from A all the way to B
<ruby>商品<rt>しょうひん</rt></ruby>からサービスに<ruby>至<rt>いた</rt></ruby>るまで

fields.connection: V volitional form + か + Vる + まいか
examples: I've been agonizing over whether or not to tell him the truth.
I plan to talk it over with my parents and decide whether to get a job or not go on to further study.
While I was hesitating over whether or not to buy it now, it sold out.
Right up to the end, I couldn't decide whether or not to return to my country.
I'm thinking about whether or not to attend the meeting.
fields.explain:
Used to emphasize the process of hesitation; suitable for essays and narration.
Goes well with verbs related to decisions:決める,迷う,悩む,考える.
This phrase is usually followed by a result/development: ～か～まいか、結局～／～と考えた。
With する: both するまいか and すまいか are seen; するまいか is preferred in modern Japanese.

• Expresses hesitation between two choices, “to do or not to do”.
• More formal than VるかVないか; has a written/speech-like tone.
• The subject is usually the speaker or the decision-maker; describes the process of deliberation.
• Sometimes used to set up the hesitation before a decision: ～か～まいか、結局…
fields.notes:
• “まい” is an old-fashioned negative volitional form; today it mainly survives in this formula and in ～まいと思う.
• In spoken language, VるかVないか is usually used instead to sound more natural.
• In titles/literature, this pattern creates a symmetrical rhythm and adds emphasis.
mistakes: Wrong form: the second part must be “Vる＋まいか” (or Vまいか with ichidan verbs), not “ないか”.
Confusing it with ～ようが～まいが (regardless) leads to the wrong meaning.
Using it in casual speech sounds stiff; the JLPT likes to test the formal nuance of this pattern.
Using different verbs in the two clauses: the same verb must be used to create the correct correspondence.

rows: <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>こうか<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くまいか<ruby>迷<rt>まよ</rt></ruby>う
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くか<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かないか<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>める
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>くだ</rt></ruby>ろうが<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>るまいが<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く
Nominalized clause; does not stress hesitation
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くかどうか<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からない
<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>うべきか<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>うべきでないか

fields.connection: Vます(drop ます) + がい (やりがい・生きがい)
examples: This project is worth learning from.
As children grow up, you feel that raising them was worth the effort.
Despite the long line, the taste was ordinary, so it wasn't worth the wait.
These are materials well worth reading for history lovers.
fields.explain:
Can take an object complement: ～をV-ます + がいがある（実習生を教えがいがある）.
Not used with purely stative verbs/verbs with no clear output.

- Emotional focus: the speaker “feels it was worth the effort”.
- Suitable for spoken language, job advertisements, and sharing experiences.
fields.notes:
• Many words combine naturally: 教えがい／鍛えがい／挑みがい／撮りがい／見がい／味わいがい.
• “見がい” exists, but “見ごたえ” is more common to express “worth seeing”. examples: 1. やりがいのある仕事
Work worth doing
2. 教えがいのある生徒
A student worth teaching
mistakes: Dropping “が” after がい: “やりがいある” → unnatural; should be “やりがいがある”.
Using it with verbs that produce no result: for example, “あるがい” is incorrect.
Confusing it with 甲斐があって: that is a result clause after the action is done; ～がいがある is a general evaluation.

rows: <ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>の<ruby>甲斐<rt>かい</rt></ruby>があった
Used when logical argument is needed
<ruby>投資<rt>とうし</rt></ruby>する<ruby>価値<rt>かち</rt></ruby>がある

fields.connection: Nが + Vられる（spontaneous・potential: 感じられる・思い出される）
examples: Sincerity can be felt in what he says.
The author's inner conflict can be glimpsed in this work.
When spring comes, the scenery of my hometown comes back to me.
Several safety issues can be observed at the site.
There are concerns about bias in the data.
This result could also be considered a coincidence.
fields.explain:
The speaker as subject is usually omitted; emphasizes a “natural/objective” quality.
The person who perceives can be added with に/には:彼には誠意が感じられた (less common than the impersonal form).
Suits a report style: ～が観察される／～が指摘される／～が確認される .

• Spontaneous passive: feelings/thoughts arise naturally, with no agent mentioned. Example verbs: 思われる・感じられる・思い出される・偲ばれる・うかがわれる・懸念される.
• Observation/recognition: describes phenomena that are seen/noticed objectively: 見られる・見受けられる・観察される・確認される.
• Nuance: objective, neutral; written language, reports, academic writing, news.
fields.notes:
• Typical spontaneous verbs: 思われる・考えられる・感じられる・思い出される・偲ばれる・うかがわれる・期待される・懸念される.
• 見られる has two meanings: “can see” (ability) and “is observed” (objective passive); distinguish them by context.
• Avoid “ら抜き言葉” in exams/writing: use the correct 考えられる, not 考えれる.
mistakes: Confusing it with the potential form: 見られる does not always mean “can see”; it can mean “is observed”.
Adding an agent with に to the spontaneous form distorts the meaning: 誠意が彼に感じられる is unnatural; say 彼の発言には誠意が感じられる instead.
Confusing it with the subjective ～ように感じる/思う; exam questions often ask you to choose the more objective form over the subjective one.

rows: <ruby>温<rt>あたた</rt></ruby>かみが<ruby>感<rt>かん</rt></ruby>じられる
Subjective; the speaker is the agent
<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>温<rt>あたた</rt></ruby>かみを<ruby>感<rt>かん</rt></ruby>じる
<ruby>増加<rt>ぞうか</rt></ruby><ruby>傾向<rt>けいこう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>られる
～ように<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>える/<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>こえる

fields.connection: Vます(drop ます) + きれる（negative: きれない）
examples: There's so much to write that I can't fit it all on this one sheet.
B: I'm sorry, it's sold out. More will come in tomorrow.

fields.meaning: Since… (giving one of several reasons); seeing as…, so…
examples: 〈A father to his son〉 Since Mom and Maki are both out today, shall we two go out for dinner?

A: What should I do? I won't finish my report in time. And since I'm not feeling well either, maybe I'll ask for tomorrow off from my part-time job.
B: Why don't you?
fields.notes: Attaches to a clause. With the structure 「ことだ＋し」, it is used to state the circumstances or situation that serve as the reason or grounds for some judgment, decision, or wish. 「ことですし」, as in ②, is a more polite form. It can be used to state two reasons, as in ③, or just one, as in ②, or tacked on at the end like an afterthought, as in ①. It is spoken language, but a more formal expression than 「し」 alone. （１１７）

fields.meaning: When it comes to… (attitude/state changes completely)
examples: He's usually quiet, but when it comes to mountain climbing, he suddenly becomes talkative.
Making a packed lunch is more economical and better for your health, but when it comes to doing it every day, it might be hard.
The main ingredient of this medicine, namely vitamin C, is lacking.
He is a speaker of three languages, that is, trilingual.
Company A and Company B are the same corporation; in other words, legally they are the same organization.
This figure is sales revenue, that is, not net income.
fields.explain:
Used in definitions, explanations of terms, and to state a relationship of identity.
Formal/academic style; つまり is more of an everyday summarizing word.
Usually accompanied by commas before/after to set off the explanatory clause.
Not used to state a result, a command, or an exclamation.

すなわち: “that is/namely/in other words (in the sense of identity)”. Used to give a definition, an exact explanation, or to restate something with an equivalent expression.
• Emphasizes a relationship of identity/equality: S2 ≒ a different expression of S1.
• More formal than つまり; leans toward precision and objectivity.
• Not used for inferring a result or for emotional summarizing.
fields.notes:
• Tip: if you could put “= (equals)” between S1 and S2, すなわち is the correct choice.
• In scientific writing it often appears in definitions: Xとは、すなわちYである。
• The kanji 即ち is rarely used today; the kana すなわち is preferred for readability. meaning_vi: In other words, that is ⏐ explain: Used when expressing something in a different way.
Similar to　「つまり」 but cannot be used when talking about a result.
財布をなくした。すなわちお金がない。（X)
→財布をなくした。つまりお金がない。（O)
Stiff sentence. ⏐ examples: 1. 「母の兄、すなわち僕のおじですが・・・・・・」
My mother's older brother, in other words my uncle…
2. このペットボトルには１０００ミリリットル、すなわち１リットルの水が入っています。
This bottle holds 1000 ml, that is, 1 liter of water.
mistakes: Confusing it with つまり: if the question requires an “identity definition” → すなわち; if it requires “summarizing/inferring” → つまり.
Using it for a result/cause and effect is incorrect: ×「雨だ。すなわち、行かない」→ use それで/だから instead.
Making S2 not equivalent to S1 makes the sentence imprecise; make sure there is a relationship of identity.

rows: Summarizes/implies a general conclusion; less formal.
<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れる。つまり、<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>わない。
Sums up the main point, with a subjective nuance.
<ruby>議論<rt>ぎろん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>長<rt>なが</rt></ruby>い。<ruby>要<rt>よう</rt></ruby>するに、<ruby>賛成<rt>さんせい</rt></ruby>だ。
Implies inference, not an identity definition.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>？ ということは、<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>だね。

examples: This novel cannot fail to move its readers.
Wrongdoing will without fail be exposed.
His sincere words are bound to touch the hearts of those who hear them.
This problem will be solved today, no matter what.
That footage will surely stir up public opinion.
fields.explain:
States a strong cause-and-effect relationship or determination: a sense of “will surely happen/will definitely do”.
Formal; suitable for commentary, speeches, and news; rarely used in everyday conversation.
Meaning A usually goes with N/人を + V-使役: “to make/drive … into state X”.
Meaning B suits contexts expressing the volition, responsibility, or determination of the speaker/organization.
Usually not used for ordinary actions with no inevitability/decisiveness.

• Meaning A (inevitable result): “Will surely/cannot fail to cause …” — a powerful agent inevitably leads to a reaction/result. Example: その演説は聴衆を魅了せずにはおかない。
• Meaning B (strong volition/determination): “Will definitely do …; will not let it go” — the speaker expresses the will to carry it through no matter what. Example: この件は必ず突き止めずにはおかない。
• Nuance: stiff, written language, journalism/commentary/speeches; decisive, close to a confident prediction or unshakable determination.
• The subject is usually a thing/event that has an impact (Meaning A) or “I/we” with determination (Meaning B).
fields.notes:
• In commentary, this pattern helps “upgrade” the certainty of a prediction, almost asserting the result.
• With Meaning A, avoid making “I” the subject unless it is a strategic statement (PR, declaration, resolution).
• A double negative is not used with this pattern; to negate it, rephrase the whole sentence with a different expression.
mistakes: Mixing it up with ～ずにはすまない: this one means “will surely cause/will definitely do”, the other means “it won't do not to (a sense of duty)”.
Using it in casual conversation → sounds forced; choose ～ずにはいられない in everyday conversation.
Unsuitable subject: for Meaning A, use a thing/work/statement as the subject to sound more natural.

rows: Formal, decisive; emphasizes inevitability or firm volition
<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>は<ruby>観客<rt>かんきゃく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>かせずにはおかない。
Sense of duty/morality; must do it to do the proper thing
<ruby>迷惑<rt>めいわく</rt></ruby>をかけたから<ruby>謝<rt>あやま</rt></ruby>らずにはすまない。
Spontaneous emotion; more colloquial; no decisive or inevitable nuance
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>曲<rt>きょく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>聴<rt>き</rt></ruby>くと<ruby>踊<rt>おど</rt></ruby>らずにはいられない。
A slightly more colloquial variant; same meaning
<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>を<ruby>感心<rt>かんしん</rt></ruby>させないではおかない。

examples: Since I broke my promise, I have no choice but to apologize.
Since we caused trouble for our customers, as a company we will probably have to give an explanation.
I lost an important document, so I have to report it to my boss.
If it turns out laws were violated, disciplinary action will have to be taken.
After all this help, I feel I have to do something to thank them.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes a “social/moral obligation”, not a burst of emotion.
To soften it, ～だろう／と思う is often used; at work it is used to affirm the responsibility to deal with something.
Not used for fun or hobbies; suits situations that call for apologizing, explaining, compensating, or handling something.

• Meaning: “It won't do/It's not right not to do it” because of moral principles, etiquette, rules, or responsibility.
• Not strong volition but the pressure of norms/circumstances that make you do it in order to settle things properly.
• Often goes with verbs such as 謝る, 連絡する, 説明する, 報告する, 対応する, 補償する, etc.
• Formal nuance; written language, work, official announcements.
fields.notes:
• Besides apologizing/explaining, this pattern suits statements of managerial responsibility: 対応せずにはすまない, 再発防止策を講じずにはすまない.
• In business emails, combine it with ものと存じます/と考えております to be polite.
• Do not overuse it in casual conversation, as it sounds “heavy with responsibility”.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～ずにはいられない: the JLPT often sets a trap between emotion (いられない) and duty (すまない).
Choosing the wrong subject/action: use it with “handling” actions involving responsibility (謝る, 説明する, 対応する...).
Not softening it in polite writing: add だろう／と思う to sound natural.
